questions.q: Why does no single log source usually show the full story of an incident?
options: A single log source always contains every event from every system
Only firewalls are capable of logging security-relevant events
Each system only logs the slice of activity it directly sees, like a sign-in or a process launch
Logs are always deleted after a few minutes
questions.explain: The firewall sees connections, identity sees sign-ins, endpoint sees process activity, and email sees messages - each is only one piece.

questions.q: In the example timeline, what event represents initial access?
options: The 9:15am remote session to the file server
The 8:47am phishing email delivery
The 9:40am archive creation
The 9:02am sign-in using credentials harvested from the phishing email
questions.explain: Initial access is the point the attacker first gained entry - the sign-in with harvested credentials, not the email itself.

questions.q: Why is timestamp normalization a necessary step before sorting events into a timeline?
options: It is only needed when fewer than two log sources are involved
Normalization deletes any event older than one hour
Timestamps are never relevant to timeline reconstruction
Logs from different systems often record time in different time zones or formats, and mismatched clocks put events in the wrong order
questions.explain: Converting every event to one consistent time zone is what makes chronological sorting actually accurate.

questions.q: What does the reconstructed timeline reveal that the same four events, listed with no particular order, would not?
options: The exact dollar cost of the incident
The attacker's name and physical location
Which event happened first, how fast the attacker moved, and the real sequence of the attack
Nothing - order has no bearing on understanding an incident
questions.explain: Chronological order turns isolated facts into a timeline that shows pacing and cause-and-effect, like staging following lateral movement by 25 minutes.

questions.q: What real IR step does a completed timeline reconstruction feed directly into?
options: Scoping the incident - checking what else the attacker touched in that same window
Skipping containment entirely
Rewriting the original alert that started the investigation
Deleting the original log sources once the timeline is built
questions.explain: Understanding the attack's real sequence is what lets an analyst ask the scoping question in Lesson 11: what else was touched in that timeframe.
